entries.title: Are orcas a kind of dolphin?
entries.answer: An orca, also called a killer whale, is the biggest member of the dolphin family. It has teeth, and what it catches depends on the group it lives with. Some groups eat mostly fish. Others hunt seals or other marine mammals. Orcas often live with relatives and use calls to stay in touch. Groups can use different calls and hunting habits, even if they live near one another. Their white patches and tall back fins make them easy to recognize.
facts: An orca is a mammal and breathes air.
The patches behind the top fins can help identify individuals.

entries.title: How can an animal make its own light?
entries.answer: Some living things can give off light by mixing chemicals inside their bodies. That light is called bioluminescence. A firefly uses flashes to signal to other fireflies. Some deep-sea fish use a shining spot to draw smaller animals closer. Other ocean animals can give off a flash when disturbed, which may distract a predator. Making a light is especially useful far below the ocean surface, where a tiny flash can stand out in the darkness.
facts: Much of the light made by ocean animals is blue or green.
A shiny object reflects light, but a bioluminescent animal makes light.

What tiny ocean drifters might make a faint flash?
How do eyes see an object that shines?

entries.title: How can deep-sea life make food without sunlight?
entries.answer: At some deep-sea vents, tiny living things can use energy from chemicals in the water to make food. They do not have to catch light from the Sun. This way of making food is called chemosynthesis. Giant tube worms can grow beside some of those vents. They have bacteria living inside them that make food, and the worms help bring the bacteria the chemicals they need. Other animals may eat bacteria or feed on animals that depend on them.
facts: Plants generally use light to make food, which is called photosynthesis.
Many other sea-floor animals still depend on bits of food falling from sunny waters.

questions.text: Where does hot, mineral-rich water come from under the sea?
How do plants use a different energy source to make food?
Why are some parts of the sea too dark for plants to grow?

entries.title: How can hungry sea otters help a kelp forest?
entries.answer: Sea otters float on their backs and can hold food above the water as they eat. Some use a stone to open a hard shell. Their diet can include crabs, clams, and sea urchins. An otter that eats urchins can reduce the number nibbling on kelp. Where that happens, kelp can grow thick enough for many other animals to shelter among its blades. An otter keeps warm with a dense coat that traps air next to its skin.
facts: Sea otters groom their coats to keep them working well.
In parts of the Pacific, sea otters are closely connected with kelp forest health.

questions.text: What kinds of animals can live under kelp?
How does a very different mammal reach small animals at mealtime?
What other habitat shelters young fish near the shore?

entries.title: How can seaweed make an underwater forest?
entries.answer: Giant kelp grows upward from rocks on the sea bottom. It is a kind of large brown algae. A tough cluster of branches holds it onto the rock. Small gas-filled floats help lift its broad blades toward the sunlight. Where many kelps grow close together, they make a shelter with levels from the floor almost to the surface. Fish can hide between the blades, and tiny animals live around the parts that grip the rocks.
facts: Sea urchins can eat kelp.
Sea otters help some kelp forests by eating sea urchins.

How is a seagrass meadow different from a kelp forest?
Why does kelp need light near the ocean surface?

entries.title: How can you tell a harbor seal from a sea lion?
entries.answer: A harbor seal has small ear openings behind its eyes, but lacks the outer ear flaps you can see on a sea lion. Its short front flippers and its rear flippers help it steer and swim. On shore, a harbor seal moves by bending and shifting its body. It cannot turn its rear flippers under itself to stride as a sea lion does. Harbor seals climb out on rocks, sandbars, or ice to rest, give birth, or shed old fur.
facts: Harbor seals can have dark spots on a light coat or light spots on a dark coat.
A seal that leaves the water to rest is said to haul out.

questions.text: Which related animal walks on its flippers on land?
Which true seal can dive very deep?
What shapes the beaches and rocky edges where seals rest?

entries.title: How do researchers recognize a right whale?
entries.answer: A North Atlantic right whale has patches of rough skin on its head. Tiny animals live on those raised spots and can make them look white. The spots make a pattern that helps people recognize individual right whales in pictures. A right whale feeds by moving slowly with its mouth open in areas crowded with small, drifting animals. Baleen lets water pass back out while food stays inside. Right whales also have no tall fin along the back.
facts: An individual right whale’s raised patches can act like a name tag in photographs.
Fishing lines and collisions with boats can injure right whales.

Which feature helps researchers tell humpbacks apart?
Which whale’s main feeding method is often along the seafloor?

entries.title: How does a bottlenose dolphin find a fish in murky water?
entries.answer: A bottlenose dolphin can see in the water, but it has another way to find food in poor light. It makes short clicks and listens for echoes that bounce back from nearby objects. An echo can tell the dolphin where a fish is even if the fish is hard to see. Dolphins often feed together in groups. A dolphin comes to the surface for air through an opening called a blowhole on top of its head.
facts: Bottlenose dolphins have rounded foreheads above short beaks.
They use sounds to find objects and also to communicate.

questions.text: How do bats find objects using sound in the air?
Which larger animal is also a dolphin?
How do our ears turn sound into signals the brain can use?

entries.title: How does a giant manta ray eat tiny food?
entries.answer: A giant manta has wide fins that look like wings as it glides through the sea. Small flaps at the front of its head help guide water into its open mouth. Inside, structures near its gills separate tiny food from the water. A manta can swim toward places where a lot of plankton collect in one patch. Its body belongs to a large fish with a skeleton made of cartilage, the material that makes the tip of a human nose flexible.
facts: Giant manta rays have mouths at the front of the head.
A giant manta can have a spread of more than twenty feet from fin to fin.

questions.text: What kinds of small living things drift in the sea?
What other large ocean animal strains tiny food from the water?
Which large sea animal uses crushing jaws?

entries.title: How does an octopus fit into a narrow hole?
entries.answer: A giant Pacific octopus has eight strong arms with suckers and a soft body. The hard beak in the center of its arms is one of the widest hard parts it must fit through an opening. It can squeeze into spaces that look too small for it at first. The octopus often hides among rocks on the floor of the northern Pacific Ocean. It can change color and make its skin look bumpier when it matches its surroundings.
facts: An octopus has arms with suckers along much of their length.
A mother octopus guards her eggs.

questions.text: Which octopus relative has a hard outside shell?

What changes as you travel down through ocean water?

entries.title: How does new seafloor form?
entries.answer: Long chains of underwater mountains rise along parts of the ocean floor. Many form where two plates move apart. Hot rock rises under the gap, and some of it melts. Fresh material that reaches the surface cools and becomes part of the seafloor. As the plates keep moving, each new strip carries older rock farther from the middle. The ridge and its two sides keep a record of changes over immense stretches of time.
facts: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs through much of the Atlantic Ocean.
Places called hydrothermal vents often form close to ridges.

questions.text: Why do the big pieces of Earth’s surface move at all?
How can hot rock under a ridge make a chimney of minerals?
Where can an old plate sink down below another plate?

entries.title: How far does sunlight reach into the ocean?
entries.answer: When you travel down through clear ocean water, the sunlight gets weaker. Near the top, enough light reaches plants and tiny algae for them to make food. Farther down, a dim band has traces of daylight, but too little for much food making by light. Deeper still, sunlight never reaches. Animals there can eat other animals or food that sinks down from above. Some can even make their own light while they move through the dark.
facts: In clear water, the sunlit upper zone can reach roughly 200 meters deep.
Deep water also presses harder on an animal than water near the surface.

questions.text: How does an animal make light where the Sun cannot reach?
How can food be made in complete darkness?
How deep do some narrow parts of the ocean floor reach?

entries.title: How tiny animals build coral reefs
entries.answer: A coral reef can look like a pile of rocks or plants, but it is built by small animals called coral polyps. Many kinds live in groups. The kinds that build reefs make hard cups around themselves. Old cups stay behind and new ones can grow on top, so a reef gets larger over time. Many reef corals also have tiny algae living inside them. The algae use sunlight to make food, and the coral gets some of that food. The reef’s holes and branches give fish and other animals places to live.
facts: A coral reef can shelter many different living things.
Heat stress can cause coral to lose its partner algae and turn pale.

questions.text: How do algae and plants use sunlight to make food?
How does ocean movement affect where warmth goes?
Why is a coral reef more than a group of animals?

entries.title: Is a narwhal’s tusk a horn?
entries.answer: A narwhal’s long spiral tusk is a tooth that grows out through its upper lip. The tusk is seen most often on males. Scientists have found tiny channels and nerves in it, so it can sense its surroundings. Narwhals live in Arctic waters. They spend time among sea ice and travel to different feeding grounds as the seasons change. They breathe air, so when sea ice covers much of the water, they need open places where they can come up to breathe.
facts: A narwhal can sometimes have two tusks.
Narwhals have a low ridge instead of a tall back fin.

questions.text: Which other light-colored whale lives in Arctic waters?
Which animal also grows tusks from teeth?
How is an orca’s back fin different from a narwhal’s ridge?

entries.title: What are a humpback whale’s bubbles for?
entries.answer: Some humpback whales make loops of bubbles under schools of fish. The bubbles crowd the fish together as they rise. One or more whales can then swim upward through the center with mouths open. Humpbacks have long front flippers and broad tails. The marks on the underside of a tail can help people tell one whale from another. Humpbacks also make many sounds. Males make long patterns of calls that people describe as songs.
facts: A humpback can slap the water with its long front flippers.
Many humpbacks move long distances between feeding areas and places where their calves are born.

questions.text: Which giant whale uses similar mouth filters to catch tiny food?
Why do groups of orcas make different calls?
What other whale makes a long trip to warmer water?

entries.title: What are plankton?
entries.answer: Plankton are living things that drift with moving water. Many are very small. Some can swim a little, but ocean currents can carry them farther than they can swim on their own. Phytoplankton use light to make food. Other plankton may eat them or catch smaller drifting animals. Even some fish or crabs begin life as plankton before they grow into animals strong enough to move in their own direction. Plankton are an important food for many larger ocean animals.
facts: Krill are among the animal plankton that whales can eat.
Some jellyfish also drift with currents and count as plankton.

questions.text: How does a very large fish strain plankton out of the sea?
Which huge whale eats masses of krill?
What happens when a kind of algae grows very fast?

entries.title: What are the chimneys on the ocean floor?
entries.answer: In some places on the sea floor, water can enter cracks in the rock. It travels close to hot rock below, heats up, and returns carrying chemicals and minerals. When this hot water meets much colder ocean water, some minerals become tiny solid pieces. Over time those pieces can pile up around the opening and grow into a chimney. The dark cloud that comes from a vent called a black smoker is mostly made of mineral particles.
facts: Some life near these vents depends on energy from chemicals.
Vent chimneys can grow even far below the part of the ocean that gets sunlight.

Where can magma heat water below the ocean floor?
How deep does light reach into ocean water?

entries.title: What can a loggerhead turtle crack with its jaws?
entries.answer: A loggerhead has a broad, heavy head with jaws strong enough to break the shells of animals such as crabs. The top of its shell is usually reddish brown. Young loggerheads can spend years offshore. As they get larger, many move to shallower water to feed near the bottom. When a nesting female returns to a beach, she digs a hole with her back flippers, lays a group of eggs, and covers the nest with sand.
facts: The loggerhead is named for its large head.
A loggerhead’s front flippers are longer than its back ones.

questions.text: How does grazing on seagrass differ from cracking a crab shell?
Which sea turtle feeds on soft jellyfish?
How does a giant ray catch tiny food without crushing shells?

entries.title: What does the biggest animal on Earth eat?
entries.answer: A blue whale can be longer than two school buses, but it mostly eats tiny animals called krill. To feed, it speeds into a patch of krill and opens its mouth wide. Folds under the jaws stretch outward to make room for water and food. Then its tongue pushes the water back out through narrow spaces. Strips called baleen catch the krill, a little like a kitchen strainer holding noodles when the cooking water drains away.
facts: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have lived.
Blue whales surface to breathe air.

Why does a gray whale dive to the seafloor when it eats?

entries.title: What happens when a river meets the sea?
entries.answer: Where a river reaches the sea, freshwater can meet water brought in by the tide. In many places the two meet in a partly enclosed area called an estuary. The water is often brackish, with more salt than river water and less than ocean water. A strong rainfall or a high tide can change how salty different parts are. Young fish, crabs, and birds find food and shelter in many estuaries where water and land meet.
facts: Salt levels can change from one end of an estuary to the other.
Some estuaries have broad, muddy areas that show when the tide falls.

questions.text: What habitat can grow along a shallow edge of an estuary?
Where can trees and shrubs thrive in coastal salt water?
How does water from the land make it down to the sea?

entries.title: What is a red tide?
entries.answer: Tiny algae are a normal part of the ocean. When some kinds get conditions that help them grow very quickly, they can form a big patch called a bloom. Some blooms make chemicals that can hurt fish, other wildlife, or people. Those harmful blooms are sometimes called red tides, though the water can have other colors or look unchanged. Other algae blooms are harmless. Scientists test water to learn which kind is there.
facts: An algal bloom may be patchy and move with currents.
The term red tide does not mean that high or low tide has arrived.

How can the ocean move a large patch of water?

entries.title: What makes a leatherback different from other sea turtles?
entries.answer: The leatherback is the largest kind of sea turtle. Its shell has long ridges and a flexible outer covering rather than the hard plates found on most other sea turtles. Leatherbacks swim across oceans and dive for soft animals such as jellyfish. Their mouths and throats have backward-facing points that help hold slippery food. A female leatherback comes ashore to bury her eggs in sand, even though she spends nearly all the rest of her time in the ocean.
facts: A leatherback can travel through colder seas than most sea turtles.
Soft plastic drifting in the sea can be mistaken for food by sea turtles.

questions.text: Why is the green turtle named for a color that is not on its shell?
Which sea turtle has crushing jaws for hard-shelled food?

entries.title: What makes a tsunami different from wind waves?
entries.answer: A tsunami starts when a great amount of ocean water is suddenly pushed out of place. An earthquake that lifts or drops part of the ocean floor can start one. Far from land it can travel very quickly, while the surface may not look unusually high to someone on a boat. Near a coast, the water gets shallower and the waves slow and may grow taller. A tsunami can bring several surges, one after another.
facts: Underwater landslides can also start tsunamis.
An ordinary ocean wave usually begins when wind moves across the surface.

How does wind make the waves seen on a normal beach?

entries.title: What makes ocean currents flow
entries.answer: An ocean current is water moving from one place to another. In shallow areas near the coast, the tide can make water flow into a bay and later flow out. Farther from land, winds can drive large streams of water near the surface. Cold or salty water is usually denser than warmer or fresher water. That difference also helps move water around, including deep below the ocean’s surface. These currents can carry heat between regions, so they help shape weather and climate on land.
facts: Winds, tides, and differences in water density all drive ocean currents.
The Gulf Stream carries warm water in the Atlantic Ocean.

questions.text: What makes the ocean rise and fall at the shore?
Why can two blocks of the same size have different densities?
How is a wave different from a flowing current?

entries.title: Where is the deepest part of the ocean?
entries.answer: The ocean floor is not flat. Long, narrow valleys called trenches cut deeply below nearby areas. The deepest known place is Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench in the western Pacific Ocean. It is about eleven kilometers below the surface. Many trenches form where one moving plate bends and slides beneath another. A person could not breathe or stand the pressure at that depth without a specially designed vessel to protect them.
facts: Sunlight does not reach the bottom of Earth’s deepest trenches.
The pressure at Challenger Deep is much greater than at the surface.

questions.text: Why can pieces of Earth’s outer layer move under each other?
How do light and pressure change as you go deeper?
What happens at a place where two plates move apart instead?

entries.title: Why can a beluga turn its head?
entries.answer: Belugas live in Arctic and nearby waters. A young beluga is gray, and most become white as they grow older. A beluga can turn and nod its head partly because several bones in its neck are not joined together the way they are in many other whales. Belugas use many whistles, chirps, and clicks. Their clicks can help them tell where fish or other objects are when they listen for sound returning from those objects.
facts: Belugas lack a tall fin on their back.
The round bump on a beluga’s head helps focus the sounds it makes.

How does another ocean mammal use returning sounds?
Can a mammal that flies also find food with echoes?

entries.title: Why can water rush away from a beach?
entries.answer: As waves break near a beach, they push water toward land. Some of that water flows back out in a narrow, fast-moving stream called a rip current. A gap between sandbanks or a place next to a pier can give it a path. The stream pulls water away from shore, rather than sucking it straight down. Even when the beach looks calm, water can move quickly in one small part of the surf.
facts: Rip currents can form on shores of large lakes as well as the ocean.
A rip current is a flow of water, rather than the rise and fall of a tide.

questions.text: How does water change as an ocean wave reaches a beach?
What causes seawater to rise and fall over hours?
How do water currents move across much bigger distances?

entries.title: Why do mangrove trees have roots above water?
entries.answer: Mangroves are trees and shrubs that grow along warm coasts, often where the tide soaks their roots with seawater. Their roots can grow into shapes that support each tree in muddy ground and help some roots get air. Under the branches, the tangle of roots gives small fish and crabs places to hide. Mangrove trees can also slow waves near the shore and help trap mud so it does not wash away as easily.
facts: Different mangrove kinds have different ways of dealing with salt.
Some mangrove roots rise above the mud like short pencils.

Where can seawater and freshwater meet near a coast?
Which animal also helps keep a coastal habitat healthy?

entries.title: Why does a gray whale roll on its side to eat?
entries.answer: A gray whale can feed by turning partly onto its side and drawing in a mouthful of water and mud near the bottom. It pushes the mud and water out through its baleen. Small animals left inside its mouth become dinner. Many gray whales live in the Pacific and travel between cold feeding grounds and warmer areas where their calves are born. A mother and her calf may head north together again when the calf can swim well enough for the journey.
facts: Gray whales often have visible patches of barnacles on their skin.
They have a low hump and bumps along the back instead of a tall back fin.

questions.text: Which other baleen whale feeds mostly on krill?
Which whale sometimes gathers fish with bubbles?
Which whale slowly strains swimming food near the surface?

entries.title: Why does a meadow of seagrass matter to fish?
entries.answer: Seagrasses are flowering plants that can live under salty water. Their roots hold onto the sea floor, and long leaves move back and forth when water passes by. Many grow in clear, shallow places where sunlight can reach down to them. A thick patch gives young fish and other animals places to hide. The roots and stems slow down the movement of mud and sand. Some sea turtles graze on the leaves.
facts: A giant kelp is an alga, while a seagrass is a flowering plant.
Seagrasses can trap particles and make water nearby clearer.

questions.text: How does seagrass become food for a hungry turtle?
How does seaweed make another kind of underwater shelter?
Which coastal grasses spend part of the day out of seawater?

entries.title: Why does a salt marsh flood twice a day in some places?
entries.answer: A salt marsh is a low, grassy wetland next to the sea. When the tide comes in, seawater covers part of it, then runs out as the tide falls. How often a spot floods depends on its height and on the tides in that area. Marsh plants can live in wet, salty mud where many other plants cannot grow. Tidal creeks wind across the marsh and carry water, food, and tiny animals from one part to another.
facts: A salt marsh gives young fish and crabs sheltered places to grow.
Marsh plants can slow waves and hold wet soil in place.

questions.text: Where does salty water often mix with water from the land?
How does a warm-shore wetland look when trees grow in it?
Why does the ocean rise and fall?

entries.title: Why is a nautilus shell divided into rooms?
entries.answer: A chambered nautilus is an ocean animal with a coiled shell divided by walls. Its soft body lives in the large room near the opening. Smaller rooms behind it contain gas and liquid. Changing the amount of liquid helps the animal stay at a useful depth without needing to swim all the time. A tube called a siphuncle connects its body to the rooms. The nautilus can pull much of its body into the outer room for protection.
facts: A nautilus is related to octopuses and squids.
It has many long tentacles, without suckers like an octopus’s.

questions.text: How can a relative that lacks a hard shell squeeze into openings?
Why can a gas-filled chamber change how something floats?
How can a shell leave an ancient record in rock?

entries.title: Why is an elephant seal named for an elephant?
entries.answer: An adult male northern elephant seal has a large nose that hangs over its mouth a little like a short trunk. It helps make the seal’s deep calls loud during the breeding season. Elephant seals spend many months at sea feeding, and they can stay underwater for a long time. Their bodies store a great deal of oxygen in blood and muscle. They come back to shore to have pups and to shed their old skin and fur.
facts: A male elephant seal is much larger than a female.
Elephant seals make deep dives to catch animals such as squid and fish.

questions.text: How does another true seal travel on land?
How does a real elephant’s long trunk work?
How does air in lungs deliver oxygen into blood?

entries.title: Why is it called a green sea turtle?
entries.answer: A green sea turtle’s name comes from the green tint of its body fat, rather than the outside of its shell. Older green turtles often graze on seagrasses and algae in shallow water. A green turtle’s front flippers pull it through the sea like paddles. Many adult females make long journeys between feeding grounds and sandy places where they lay eggs. The young hatch on shore and cross the sand to enter the water.
facts: Green sea turtles eat mostly plants and algae after they grow larger.
Seagrass beds are places where green turtles can find food.

questions.text: What does a sea turtle with a heavy head eat?
How is a leatherback’s shell different?
What other kind of plant habitat grows near the sea?

entries.title: Why the ocean has tides
entries.answer: If you leave a stick on the beach, later waves might reach it even though the wind has not changed. The water level rises and falls as part of the tide. The Moon’s pull on Earth and the ocean is a major cause, and the Sun’s pull matters too. The water does not go up and down by the same amount on every shore. The shape of the coast and depth of the water make a difference. Many places have two high tides and two low tides in about a day.
facts: High tide and low tide are different water levels.
A tide can also make water flow sideways through a narrow channel.

questions.text: What is gravity, and how can the Moon pull on Earth?
How are shore waves different from the tide?
What else besides tides can make ocean water flow?

entries.title: Why there are waves in the ocean
entries.answer: Many ocean waves begin when wind pushes on the water’s surface. The pushes add energy. That energy can travel a long way as a wave, even when much of the water just moves around its own small area. Near a beach, waves slow down as the water gets shallower. Their tops can tip forward and break, making the white water you see at the shore. A different kind of wave, called a tsunami, can start when the ocean is suddenly disturbed, such as when an earthquake moves the sea floor.
facts: Wind waves can travel far from the place where the wind made them.
Where waves break, they can stir up and move sand.

How can an earthquake move solid ground under the water?
Where does sand go when it is carried away?
